notes: Re-review after merging current main into this branch (merge commit 5a036df, zero conflicts — main's newer website work and this branch's Content Machine work both preserved) and after fixing a REAL DEFECT found by inspecting the rendered frames, described next. Bound to the freshly rendered bytes at masterSha256 9e0e58bf...cad7e22, produced by offlineGeneratedPlanRender.ts rendering the same real generated six-beat production plan for compare-rtx4080s-rtx4080. All seven frames re-extracted with ffmpeg at the same timestamps as the prior review and committed alongside this file (frameRefs).

DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED THIS ROUND — the deterministic-ui-render capability was not deterministic. Inspecting the frames of the previous render showed beats 2-4 with fully drawn FPS bars and their numeric value labels, and beats 5-6 with SHORTER bars and NO value labels: five beats requesting the byte-identical capture spec had produced two different images (md5 d6161d14... for three of them, 7ace8cac... for the other two). Root cause, measured rather than guessed: Compare's per-game chart is Recharts, which animates bar geometry from its own JS timer and mounts the <LabelList> values only when that animation finishes. That is not a CSS animation or transition, so neither capture.ts's FREEZE_ANIMATIONS_CSS nor Playwright's animations:"disabled" stopped it, and because the bars grow HORIZONTALLY the old settle condition — two animation frames of equal document.body HEIGHT — never saw it. Instrumented against the running build: at the instant the old check passed, the chart had 40 rendered elements and bars at ~114px; 200ms later, 80 elements and ~121px; stable only around 420ms. Whether a screenshot landed before or after that was pure timing.

TWO-PART FIX, each verified separately. (1) uiRender/capture.ts's settle condition #3 now compares a signature of every laid-out element's rounded position and size — so both moving geometry and late-appearing nodes register — sampled across six consecutive animation frames, all of which must match; it stays a DOM condition, never a sleep, and a page still moving at the timeout now fails loudly as layout-never-settled. (2) Compare.tsx's two <Bar>s now pass isAnimationActive={!prefersReducedMotion} via the new src/hooks/usePrefersReducedMotion.ts. That second half is a genuine accessibility fix in its own right — index.css already honours prefers-reduced-motion for every CSS animation, but a JS-driven library animation escaped it, so a viewer who asked for no motion still got a 1.5s animated chart — and it is what makes the capture deterministic BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by out-waiting a race, since the capture context sets reducedMotion:"reduce". Measured directly: under reducedMotion:"reduce" the chart is at final geometry with all 80 elements present on the very first frame after load (no animation at all); under no-preference it still animates from 49px to 121px over ~390ms, so the animation is preserved for viewers who want it.

HONEST ATTRIBUTION OF THE TWO HALVES: with the Compare.tsx half reverted and only the capture.ts settle fix in place, three consecutive renders still produced consistent, correctly-settled captures — so the capture.ts fix is the one demonstrably observed to resolve the defect. The Compare.tsx half was NOT observed to change the render output on its own; it is kept because it removes the residual race at its source (a stability check can still pass in a quiet window BEFORE an animation begins, which was observed once during diagnosis) and because it fixes the reduced-motion accessibility gap independently. Neither claim is stated more strongly than that.

REGRESSION COVER ADDED, both proven to fail without their fix. src/hooks/usePrefersReducedMotion.test.tsx covers the hook (stated preference, no preference, a change mid-session, listener cleanup on unmount, and the no-matchMedia prerender environment) and asserts structurally — after stripping comment lines, so prose cannot satisfy the check — that Compare.tsx calls the hook and that EVERY <Bar> passes isAnimationActive={!prefersReducedMotion}, not just the first; removing the prop fails it. offlineGeneratedPlanRender.ts now also refuses the render outright if two tasks reporting the same adapter stateId produced different image bytes, so this class of bug can never again pass silently into a video.

REAL LIMITATION, not scored around: beats 2 through 6 (5 of the video's 6 beats) show the IDENTICAL captured Compare-page state — productionPlan.ts's deriveUiRenderState derives one static UI state per plan and every non-hook beat reuses it. That is now literally true and enforced (see the stateId guard above), where before it was asserted while two of the five actually differed. It remains a weak asset for 22 of 25 seconds and is reflected honestly in visualCoherenceScore/pacingScore below rather than inflated.

No fake or generated UI is presented as real anywhere: the one non-UI beat (the hook) is a plain, clearly labeled offline fixture card. No fabricated benchmark or price data — every number in the real-UI beats is the app's own estimateFpsForBuild()/gpus.json/cpus.json output, and every dollar figure is explicitly labeled Est. on screen.

AUDIO — signal analysis only, NOT a listen. This environment has no audio playback capability and no agent in it can hear the file, so audioReviewMethod stays "signal-analysis-only" and the quality gate correctly refuses a passing audio verdict on that basis alone, regardless of audioClarityScore. Measured over the full 25.338s master of THESE exact bytes: stream is AAC 22050Hz mono, 25.338005s, against a 25.333s h264 1080x1920 30fps video stream. ffmpeg silencedetect (noise=-35dB, d=0.3s) reported ZERO silence intervals — narration continuous, no dropouts. ffmpeg volumedetect: mean_volume -21.7dB, max_volume -2.0dB. ffmpeg ebur128: integrated -21.5 LUFS, loudness range 1.3 LU, true peak -2.0 dBFS. Two honest observations a listener should check: -21.5 LUFS is roughly 7 LU quieter than the ~-14 LUFS short-form platforms normalise toward, and a 1.3 LU range is extremely flat — both consistent with synthetic espeak-ng narration rather than a human read. A genuine full listen by someone with playback capability is still required before audioReviewMethod can become "listened-full" for these exact bytes.

REPRODUCIBILITY — a prior review round recorded that rendered bytes are 'not reproducible run to run even for identical source' and attributed that to ffmpeg. That now looks like it was at least partly a MISDIAGNOSIS of the racing UI capture described above: with the capture fixed, THREE consecutive full renders on this machine at this commit produced the byte-identical master 9e0e58bf...cad7e22, and all five same-spec UI captures came out at md5 d6161d14... every time. This is evidence about ONE machine only and does NOT establish cross-machine reproducibility — a CI runner has a different ffmpeg build, different fonts and a different Chromium, any of which can change the bytes — so the evidence gate in endToEndOfflinePipeline.ts remains bound to this one sha256 and is still expected to report NO MATCH elsewhere. The content-e2e-offline.yml header's claim that non-reproducibility is inherent to ffmpeg should be treated as unproven, not as established fact.
